messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format) for writing LLM prompts. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 students, prompts built with the template scored higher on three predefined tasks (mean 0.74 vs 0.61) and raised participants' confidence, but took slightly longer.

sections.title: What the paper proposes
sections.text: The authors present PromptScaffold, which splits a prompt into role, task, examples and output format slots, each with a short hint and example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that users can preview and edit freely.

sections.title: Main findings of the study
sections.text: Across three tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling and news summarisation), template prompts reached higher automatic task scores, with the largest gain on topic labelling. Participants reported higher confidence with the template (4.1 vs 3.4 on a 7-point scale) and took somewhat longer (7.5 vs 6.2 minutes), according to the paper's results table as described by PaperLens.

sections.title: Limits the authors name
sections.text: The authors stress a small, homogeneous sample of university students, a single 70-minute session, three predefined tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence. They also note that participants often filled slots mechanically without understanding why they mattered.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your study
sections.text: Because your project studies how non-expert users write prompts, the paper's slot-based scaffold and its observation that users filled slots mechanically could inform the design of your user study conditions. You could consider whether a comparison with a plain text box, and measures beyond automatic scores and self-report, would suit your research questions.

sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.
quotes: We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format.

sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.
quotes: Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1).

sources.text: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format) to write LLM prompts. It reports a within-subjects lab study with 16 university students who completed three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling, news summarisation) under free-form and template conditions. Prompts written with the template achieved a higher mean automatic task score (0.74 vs 0.61) and higher self-rated confidence (4.1 vs 3.4), at the cost of slightly more time. The authors note that participants often filled slots mechanically and that the study's small, homogeneous sample, single session, single LLM and automatic metrics limit generalisability.

2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists.

It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results.

sections.title: Limitations the authors name
sections.text: The authors list three limitations: the sample was small and homogeneous, each participant used the tool in one 70-minute session, and only three predefined tasks and one LLM were tested. They also measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence, and note that open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings might give different results.

sections.title: Mechanical slot filling as a design limit
sections.text: The authors report that several participants filled the slots mechanically because the tool did not explain why each part mattered. This points to a limitation of the template design itself, not only of the sample, and the authors suggest explaining each slot's purpose and letting users drop slots that do not fit.

messages.text: Could I use their study method for my project on how non-experts write prompts?

messages.short_answer: Partly. The paper's design (within-subjects comparison, counterbalanced conditions, parallel task versions, an automatic score, a confidence rating, time logging and a closing interview) could be adapted for your study. However, it measures prompt quality and confidence rather than how non-experts write prompts, so you would need to add process measures.

sections.title: Design elements you could reuse
sections.text: The authors compared free-form prompting with the template in a within-subjects design, counterbalanced the condition order and used parallel task versions so no participant saw the same inputs twice. They also logged time to the final prompt and ended each session with a short interview.

sections.title: What the method captures and what it misses
sections.text: The main outcome is an automatic task score, so the study shows whether the final prompts worked, not how people arrived at them. Your question about how non-experts write prompts would need data on the writing process, such as think-aloud sessions, screen or edit logs, or analysis of drafts. The paper's own observation that several participants filled the slots mechanically suggests that process data could reveal something the score cannot.

sections.title: Possible adaptations for your user study
sections.text: You could keep the counterbalanced within-subjects structure and parallel tasks, but add process measures such as think-aloud protocols and draft-level analysis. The interview could be expanded to probe how users decide what to state, which is closer to your research question. The paper does not report what its interviews found, so you would need to design your own interview guide.

Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.
